subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage: “Ankita, sit. You told your friends that a deadline sharpens you, and I, Bhupen, said it too, once. Third year of engineering, every project done on the last night, and it mostly worked, so I believed it. For my final thesis I planned the same: start on the night before the deadline. Two days before, I woke with a high fever and a body that would not stand. There was no last night to use. I lay in bed, frantic, while my roommate carried water to me. The department was kind about an extension, but the work I finally submitted was thin, and it taught me that all those last nights had only been luck, not a skill.”

qa.q: In which year of engineering did Bhupen begin doing projects on the last night?
qa.a: In the third year of engineering, Bhupen did every project on the last night.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel lying in bed with a fever two days before the deadline?
qa.a: Bhupen felt frantic and helpless, because the plan depended on a last night that could not now be used.

qa.q: What went wrong with Bhupen's plan, and what did it reveal?
qa.a: An unexpected fever ruined the plan of starting the night before, and the thin thesis showed that leaving things late had been luck, not a skill.

qa.q: How might Ankita react to hearing Bhupen's story?
qa.a: Ankita may feel startled and reflective, since Ankita also trusts deadlines to sharpen the mind, and might now see the risk in the habit.

grounding: A college student works best under pressure and leaves things to the last day, but one illness breaks the plan.

subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage: “Nine hours left,” Elizabeth said, tapping her laptop. “I work best under pressure.” Nazia, her roommate, glanced at the clock and at the empty document. At 2 pm the campus internet crashed. Elizabeth ran to the library, found every table taken, and typed on the staircase with the laptop on her knees. At 4:20 she attached the file, but the charts were missing, and the conclusion ended mid-sentence. She submitted at 4:58 anyway, and lay on her bed, exhausted, with a headache. “It'll be fine,” she said. But she had not slept the night before, and she knew the essay was not what she had meant it to be. Nazia handed her some water and said nothing.

qa.q: At what time did the campus internet crash?
qa.a: The campus internet crashed at 2 pm.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she said “It'll be fine”?
qa.a: Elizabeth was exhausted and uneasy, trying to reassure herself, while knowing the essay was not what she had meant.

qa.q: What went wrong on the last day, and what did it show about working under pressure?
qa.a: The internet crash and a crowded library left no slack, and the essay went in with missing charts and an unfinished conclusion, showing the habit has costs.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel while handing over water and saying nothing?
qa.a: Nazia is probably sympathetic and a little worried, having seen the pattern, but chooses kindness over saying “I told you so”.

grounding: A college student who says they work best under pressure leaves work to the last day, and quality and sleep suffer.

subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage: Samir, twenty, always said he worked best under pressure. His marketing case study, worth a third of the term grade, was due on Friday at noon. He planned to write it on Thursday night, as always. On Wednesday evening, he got a fever. By Thursday he could barely sit up. His roommate Shankar brought him soup and asked, "Should I email the professor?" Samir shook his head. "I'll manage tonight." He managed four hundred words of the three thousand before his eyes closed. Shankar emailed the professor anyway, with Samir's permission, the next morning. The professor granted two days, but docked ten percent for late notice.

qa.q: How much of the term grade was the case study worth?
qa.a: It was worth a third of the term grade.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he shook his head at Shankar?
qa.a: He felt stubborn and still hopeful, clinging to the belief that he could manage under pressure even while ill.

qa.q: What went wrong with Samir's approach?
qa.a: Leaving everything to the last night left no room for a surprise like a fever, so he lost marks for late notice.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel watching Samir struggle?
qa.a: Shankar seems worried and caring, bringing soup and wanting to email the professor early to protect Samir.

grounding: Shows a student who claims to work best under pressure and leaves things to the last day, until illness breaks the plan.

subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage: In a Pune college canteen, Hafsa stirred her tea. "I'm a last-minute person," she told her friend Hansa. "My brain only works under pressure." Hansa, who planned everything, raised an eyebrow. "How did the economics project go?" "B plus. Fine." "You could have got an A. You told me you skipped the last section." Hafsa shrugged, but her smile slipped. She thought of the three nights that month she'd slept four hours, the headache that had followed her through the week, the typo in her title. "It works," she said, less sure now. "Sometimes." Hansa pushed a sticky note across the table: "Start dates?" Hafsa picked it up.

qa.q: What grade did Hafsa get on the economics project?
qa.a: She got a B plus.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's smile slipping suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and less sure, remembering the lost sleep, headache and typo that the rush had cost.

qa.q: What small step could help Hafsa use the sticky note?
qa.a: She could write a start date for each upcoming project, a few days before the deadline, and keep the last day for checking.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Hafsa's claim about pressure?
qa.a: Hansa, who plans everything, sees it as costing Hafsa marks and sleep, and gently challenges it.

grounding: Shows a student who says she works best under pressure beginning to see the cost to quality and sleep.

subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage:
Jagdish: "Ramesh, the robotics demo is tomorrow and you haven't touched the code."
Ramesh: "Relax. I work better under pressure. Tonight's the night."
Jagdish: "Last time you said that, you pulled an all-nighter and slept through the viva."
Ramesh: "And I still passed."
Jagdish: "Barely. And you were ill for three days after."
Ramesh: "That was a one-off."
Jagdish: "The motor controller broke last week. What if something breaks tonight?"
Ramesh: (pauses) "Then... I'm stuck."
Jagdish: "Right. So what's the plan?"
Ramesh: "Fine. I'll start the code now and test by ten. If something breaks, we still have time."
Jagdish: "Now you're talking."

qa.q: What happened to Ramesh after the last all-nighter?
qa.a: Ramesh slept through the viva and was ill for three days after.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling during the pause after Jagdish's question?
qa.a: Ramesh felt a flicker of worry, realising that if something broke that night there would be no way out.

qa.q: Which choice at the end is wiser, and why?
qa.a: Starting the code now and testing by ten leaves time to recover if something breaks.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see Ramesh's pressure habit?
qa.a: Jagdish sees it as risky, pointing out the missed viva and illness, and pushes Ramesh to start earlier.

grounding: A dialogue shows a student relying on last-minute pressure, and a friend pointing out its cost to sleep, health and quality.

subtype: Pressure as fuel and its cost [Actor]
passage: I used to say it proudly: I'm Deepika, and I work best with my back against the wall. In second year it mostly held. Lab reports written at midnight, a presentation stitched together on the bus. Grades were fine, not great, and I told myself fine was the price of freedom. Then came the illustration portfolio, twelve plates, due Monday. My plan was Saturday and Sunday, nonstop. On Friday night I woke up shivering with a fever and spent the weekend in bed, barely able to hold a cup. Charu brought soup and asked, gently, how many plates I had. Two. I submitted two and an apology note. Charu had finished hers the week before and spent that Sunday just fixing colours. I still think about that difference.

qa.q: How many plates did the illustration portfolio need?
qa.a: Twelve plates.

qa.q: How does Deepika feel looking back on that weekend?
qa.a: Deepika seems regretful and humbled; the old pride in working with a back against the wall has turned into a quiet sting about the difference with Charu.

qa.q: What could Deepika do differently with the next big project?
qa.a: Deepika could start plates in the week before and treat the last weekend as polishing time, so one bad illness would not wipe out the whole plan.

qa.q: What was it like for Charu to hear that only two plates were done?
qa.a: Charu was probably worried and sympathetic, having finished early; Charu asked gently rather than judging, which suggests she cared how Deepika was coping.

grounding: Shows a student who relies on last-minute pressure, gets fine but not great results, and sees an unexpected illness break the whole plan.
